meta.title: Who really said "Catch a man a fish, and you can sell it to him. Teach a man to fish, and you ruin a wonderful business opportunity"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Wikiquote files this fish-and-business joke under Karl Marx's misattributed quotes. Its only cited appearance is a 2003 humour book. Marx died in 1883.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Catch a man a fish, and you can sell it to him. Teach a man to fish, and you ruin a wonderful business opportunity'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Marx. Wikiquote lists it as misattributed, citing only a 2003 humour book — and the proverb it parodies isn't documented until 1885, after Marx died.

answer.label: Not Karl Marx — an anonymous modern joke
answer.authorDates: Origin undocumented · a modern parody of an 1885 proverb
answer.sourceLine: No work of Marx’s contains this line. Wikiquote lists it among his misattributed quotations ↗, and the only appearance it cites is a 2003 humour book, W. C. Privy’s Original Bathroom Companion, where the credit to Marx is noted as “possibly in jest.” The proverb the joke inverts — give a man a fish, teach a man to fish — is not documented in English until 1885 ↗, two years after Marx’s death, so he could not have been parodying it. Whoever wrote the gag has never been identified.

source.heading: What the record actually shows

docMeta.dd: None. No Marx work, letter or speech contains this wording.

source.excerpt: Catch a man a fish, and you can sell it to him. Teach a man to fish, and you ruin a wonderful business opportunity.
trail: Wikiquote’s Karl Marx page ↗ places this exact sentence in its Misattributed section, with the note that it was “attributed to Marx (possibly in jest)” in W. C. Privy’s Original Bathroom Companion (2003).

That book is real and datable: Open Library’s catalogue record ↗ gives W. C. Privy’s Original Bathroom Companion by Erin Barrett and Jack Mingo, St. Martin’s Griffin, New York, 2003, 478 pages — a compilation of jokes and trivia, not a source on Marx.

Quote Investigator’s study of the parent proverb ↗ finds its earliest fishing-form attestation in Anne Isabella Thackeray Ritchie’s 1885 novel Mrs. Dymond — “if you give a man a fish he is hungry again in an hour” — and never mentions Marx at all. Marx died on 14 March 1883 ↗, two years earlier.

Quote Investigator has not investigated the joke itself: a search of QI for the phrase ↗ returns nothing, so no earlier author has been traced. Meanwhile quote aggregators such as AZQuotes ↗ carry it under Marx’s name with no citation of any kind.
source.excerptNote: There is no fuller context to give: the line has no documented original setting. It circulates as a free-floating one-liner, and the earliest appearance anyone has cited for it is a 2003 book of bathroom humour that already presents it as a Marx quotation.
source.rightsNote: No rights status can honestly be asserted, because the wording has no identified author or first publication. The earliest appearance cited by Wikiquote is W. C. Privy’s Original Bathroom Companion (St. Martin’s Griffin, 2003), which is itself in copyright, but that book is a compilation and there is no evidence it originated the line. Treat the quotation as of unknown provenance rather than public domain.

author.name: Karl Marx
author.kicker: The name the joke got pinned to
author.heading: Who Karl Marx actually was
author.metaLine: 1818–1883 · German philosopher, political theorist & revolutionary socialist
author.bio: Karl Marx was a German philosopher, social and political theorist and revolutionary socialist, born in Trier in 1818 and buried in London in 1883. His major works — The Communist Manifesto (1848, with Friedrich Engels) and Das Kapital (volume I, 1867) — analysed capitalism as a system that extracts surplus value from labour. He is a magnet for invented quotations precisely because so many modern one-liners about money sound vaguely like something he might have said.

misattribution.heading: Why this one sticks to Marx
misattribution.intro: The joke is a capitalist punchline wearing a communist’s name. It sounds like Marx because it says out loud what he spent three volumes arguing — that profit depends on someone else’s dependence — and that resemblance has been enough to keep it circulating under his name for over two decades.

items.why: Wikiquote files it under Misattributed ↗, noting it was “attributed to Marx (possibly in jest)” in a 2003 book of bathroom humour. Aggregators repeat the credit without any citation — AZQuotes gives the line to Marx with no source at all ↗.

A second wording — “Sell a man a fish, he eats for a day, teach a man how to fish, you ruin a wonderful business opportunity” — circulates on Goodreads under Marx’s name ↗ with no book or source given. The site itself notes that quotations there are community-added and unverified.

items.who: Lao-Tzu, Maimonides, or “an old Chinese proverb”
items.why: The straight version has its own attribution problem. Quote Investigator ↗ traces newspaper claims calling it Chinese, Italian, Navajo and Lao-Tzu’s, and finds the earliest fishing-form wording in an 1885 English novel instead.

misattribution.truthLine: Nobody knows who wrote this joke. What is documented is that Wikiquote treats the Marx credit as an error ↗, and that the proverb it depends on postdates Marx’s death by two years.

context.heading: What Marx really said about fishing
lead: Marx did write a famous sentence about fishing, and it is the opposite of this one in spirit. In The German Ideology, drafted with Engels in 1845–46 but not published until 1932, he imagines a society in which nobody is trapped in a single trade: it “makes it possible for me to do one thing today and another tomorrow, to hunt in the morning, fish in the afternoon ↗, rear cattle in the evening, criticise after dinner.” Fishing there is freedom, not a revenue stream.

The fake quotation works as a joke because it compresses a real Marxian argument into a boardroom voice — and that compression is exactly what makes it modern. The vocabulary of “a wonderful business opportunity” belongs to the age of the management aphorism, not to a nineteenth-century Prussian in the British Museum Reading Room.
context.detailsSummary: The chronology, and what Wikiquote does not claim
detailsBody: The chronology is the cleanest disproof available. Quote Investigator’s survey finds the earliest fishing version of the proverb in Anne Isabella Thackeray Ritchie’s Mrs. Dymond (1885): “if you give a man a fish he is hungry again in an hour. If you teach him to catch a fish you do him a good turn.” Marx died on 14 March 1883. A parody cannot precede the thing it parodies.

It is worth being precise about what Wikiquote does and does not claim. It does not say the 2003 humour book invented the line — only that this is where the attribution to Marx has been located in print. The joke may well be older in spoken or online circulation; no researcher has published an earlier trace of it.
context.pull: Fishing, for Marx, was what you did in the afternoon because you were free — not what you sold someone in the morning.

sourcesVerified.claim: Wikiquote's Karl Marx page lists "Catch a man a fish, and you can sell it to him. Teach a man to fish, and you ruin a wonderful business opportunity." in its Misattributed section, with the note "Attributed to Marx (possibly in jest) in W. C. Privy's Original Bathroom Companion (2003)."

Quote Investigator's article on "Give a Man a Fish..." gives the earliest fishing-form attestation as Anne Isabella Thackeray Ritchie's 1885 novel Mrs. Dymond ("if you give a man a fish he is hungry again in an hour. If you teach him to catch a fish you do him a good turn"), traces later claims of Chinese, Italian, Navajo and Lao-Tzu origin, and does not mention Karl Marx anywhere.

Wiktionary states the proverb was "Apparently coined by Anne Isabella Thackeray Ritchie in her 1885 novel Mrs. Dymond," cites the August 1885 Macmillan's Magazine wording, and lists no Karl Marx or business-opportunity variant.

The Marxists Internet Archive text of The German Ideology (1845) contains: "to hunt in the morning, fish in the afternoon, rear cattle in the evening, criticise after dinner, just as I have a mind, without ever becoming hunter, fisherman, herdsman or critic."

Open Library's catalogue record for ISBN 031228750X gives W.C. Privy's Original Bathroom Companion by Erin Barrett and Jack Mingo, publisher St. Martin's Griffin, publish date 2003, 478 pages, first edition published in New York.

Wikipedia gives Karl Marx's dates as 5 May 1818 - 14 March 1883, born in Trier, describes him as "a German philosopher, social and political theorist, and revolutionary socialist," dates Das Kapital Volume I to 1867, and states The German Ideology was written 1845-1846 and first published in 1932.
AZQuotes presents "Catch a man a fish, and you can sell it to him. Teach a man to fish, and you ruin a wonderful business opportunity." attributed to Karl Marx with no source citation of any kind.

Goodreads carries the variant wording "Sell a man a fish, he eats for a day, teach a man how to fish, you ruin a wonderful business opportunity" attributed to Karl Marx with no book or source given, alongside the site's disclaimer that quotes are community-added and not verified.
A search of Quote Investigator's own site for "ruin a wonderful business opportunity" returns no articles - the results page reads "Nothing Found" - showing QI has not investigated this quotation.
